title: When America's Golden Couple Chose Butter Chicken: Travis Kelce, Taylor Swift, and the Quiet Triumph of Indian Fine Dining
excerpt: The NFL star called Gymkhana's food 'f***ing remarkable' — and inadvertently gave Indian cuisine's global prestige campaign its biggest endorsement yet
body:
Travis Kelce does not, by his own cheerful admission, know his dal makhani from his paneer tikka. But after a date night at Gymkhana — the two-Michelin-starred Indian restaurant tucked into Mayfair's Albemarle Street — the Kansas City Chiefs tight end has declared Indian food "f***ing remarkable." For an American athlete whose culinary comfort zone reportedly centres on steak and barbecue, this represents something approaching a paradigm shift. For Indian cuisine's long campaign for global prestige, it represents something rather more significant.

The dinner, part of a whirlwind London trip with Taylor Swift that also included a West End production of *Romeo & Juliet* starring Sadie Sink and a stop at Gordon Ramsay's Lucky Cat, saw Kelce gravitating toward the classics. Chicken tikka masala and butter chicken were, in his assessment, "damn good." He opted for milder spice levels — a concession to a palate still in training — and confessed he "had no idea what he was ordering." His brother Jason, speaking on their podcast, credited Swift with expanding Travis's culinary horizons: she was, apparently, the one who suggested they try Indian.

## The Gymkhana Effect

That the venue was Gymkhana is not incidental. Founded in 2013 by the Sethi siblings — the family behind the JKS Restaurants group that also brought London Hoppers, BAO, and Lyle's — Gymkhana earned its first Michelin star within a year of opening and became the first Indian restaurant in London to hold two stars when the second arrived in 2024. Named after the social clubs of colonial India, it serves North Indian cuisine with the kind of ingredient obsession and technical precision that the Michelin system rewards: wild muntjac biryani, kid goat methi keema, duck egg bhurji with lobster.

The restaurant's rise mirrors a broader transformation in how Indian food is positioned in global dining culture. For decades, Indian cuisine in the West occupied a peculiar liminal space: beloved as takeaway and late-night fuel, yet rarely afforded the reverence granted to French, Japanese, or Nordic cooking. The Sethi family's empire — along with peers like Darjeeling Express's Asma Khan and the team behind Dishoom — has methodically dismantled that hierarchy. Gymkhana's tasting menu runs to £120; its waiting list stretches months in advance. The food is unambiguously Indian, and unambiguously fine dining.

## Soft Power on a Plate

When America's most-discussed couple chooses an Indian restaurant as a highlight of their European getaway — and the NFL's biggest star calls the experience "remarkable" on a podcast with millions of listeners — the marketing value is incalculable. No advertising campaign could purchase the association of Indian cuisine with aspiration, romance, and cultural prestige that a single Kelce-Swift dinner provides.

For the Indian diaspora, this is simultaneously gratifying and familiar. NRIs in London, New York, Toronto, and Sydney have watched the slow-motion elevation of their culinary heritage from "ethnic food" to culinary destination with a mixture of pride and bemusement. The flavours are not new; the reverence is. What Gymkhana — and now its celebrity clientele — has accomplished is not the invention of a cuisine but the correction of a perception.

The restaurant's approach resonates with a younger generation of diaspora Indians who have grown up navigating dual identities. Gymkhana does not simplify Indian cooking for Western palates or apologise for its complexity. It presents tandoori lamb chops and Malabar parathas with the same confidence that a Parisian bistro presents its steak frites. The implicit message — that Indian food does not need adaptation to deserve Michelin stars — has been heard by a global audience that now includes two of its most visible members.

## Beyond Butter Chicken

Gordon Ramsay, for his part, called hosting Swift and Kelce at Lucky Cat "an honour" and praised the couple as "classy" and "in high spirits." But it is telling that when Kelce was asked about the most surprising part of the London trip, he did not cite Ramsay's restaurant. He cited the Indian one.

For the Sethi family and the generation of Indian-origin restaurateurs who have fought to elevate their cuisine, this is a form of recognition that arrives not through critics' awards but through the culture itself. A seat at the global table — literal and figurative — that has been earned one tandoori lamb chop, one lobster bhurji, one "damn good" butter chicken at a time.

Travis Kelce may not yet know his way around an Indian menu. But he knows what he likes. And what he likes, it turns out, is what millions of Indians have known all along.
